The White House initially established 10% tariffs on imports from all countries, along with higher “reciprocal” tariffs targeting nations such as China, Vietnam and members of the European Union that levy tariffs on U.S. goods. Mexico and Canada — Georgia’s top export destinations — were spared from the new tariffs. [...] In 2024, the Peach State ranked seventh nationwide in net exports, shipping around $53.1 billion in locally made products overseas while importing about $145.6 billion, according to the Georgia Chamber of Commerce.

President Donald Trump’s newly unveiled tariffs have sent shockwaves through the manufacturing, technology and agricultural sectors across the country — particularly in Georgia. [...] Chinese tariffs could especially affect local businesses, the Georgia chamber noted. China was the third largest buyer of local goods last year at $3 billion, behind Canada and Mexico, and the second highest importer to Georgia at $17.2 billion.

On April 3, the chamber published a report outlining the impacts local industries may experience from the tariffs, including higher prices for car parts and steel, a squeeze on crop imports and possible slowdowns at the state’s bustling ports.

results.content:
Now let’s discuss tariffs for a bit, and let’s consider duties on imported goods. If the US places a 10% tariff on a bundle of goods (perhaps a specific category of goods from a specific set of countries), then importers of those goods must pay a customs duty on the declared goods before they can be moved into the US (so-called customs-clearing). As many have noted already, these importers-of-record are firms doing business in the US (or individuals) that have arranged for the importation. [...] for a few reasons. The first is that unlike a sales tax, a tariff on imported goods occurs upstream of the point-of-sale. Instead, tariffs create increases in supply chain costs for importers, and the impact of tariffs on consumers depends on what happens as a result of these cost increases.   The last time the US imposed sweeping global tariffs, manufacturing supply chains adapted to soften the blow. The current tariff shock is stronger than in 2018, yet uncertainty is also much higher. So what will current tariffs do to supply chains? [...] Trump’s New Tariffs: What Businesses Need to Know About the Trade War’s Next Chapter The tariff spotlight is back. From 1st November, the US will impose a 25% tariff on imported medium and heavy-duty trucks—part of a broader strategy by President Trump to use tariffs as a geopolitical tool. The rationale? Tariffs, he claims, help “prevent wars.” But the global reaction has been swift. Key allies including Mexico, Canada, Japan, and Germany are pushing back, raising concerns about supply chain [...] “Tariffs are back,” the real story is this: The people these tariffs were supposed to hurt aren’t feeling the pain. The ones getting crushed are the honest, smaller American businesses. And unless you have a real strategy for how to move your supply chain out of China, you’re going to feel it even more. #tariffs #supplychain #china #logistics #manufacturing #compliance #globalsourcing
